content: Many of the techniques discussed in this text are applicable in both hospital-based and prehospital settings. However, since much of the provided examples and experiences are derived from hospital environments, it is important to address specific considerations for prehospital trauma care. Key aspects of prehospital trauma care include the presence of trained personnel with skills appropriate to the severity of the emergency, effective airway management (including endotracheal intubation where applicable), spinal immobilization, and the evaluation of prehospital care’s contribution to reducing preventable deaths. Quality improvement (QI) initiatives in prehospital settings should also consider the use of EMS run sheets, critical incident reviews (similar to in-hospital morbidity and mortality reviews), and periodic assessments of common conditions, such as motor vehicle crashes, with follow-up data from hospitals. To enhance prehospital care, corrective actions may include retraining in basic prehospital care, introducing or modifying procedures, orienting staff to new equipment or medications, and providing feedback from audits, direct observations, and case reviews. These QI efforts can be applied to individual EMS services or across broader networks, and they may also be integrated into hospital QI programs to monitor prehospital care as part of the overall care continuum. QI processes often carry legal implications. In most legal systems, QI records and discussions are considered confidential and legally protected, ensuring that they cannot be publicly disclosed or subpoenaed. This confidentiality fosters openness and honesty in reporting errors and problems. Medical records and trauma registries play a critical role in supporting QI processes. For morbidity and mortality conferences, basic medical records often suffice, but more functional systems are needed for retrospective reviews, such as preventable death panels. In many settings, inadequate documentation has hindered QI efforts, highlighting the need to improve trauma care documentation, particularly in the early phases of care. Enhanced record-keeping should be seen as beneficial and not overly burdensome for care providers. Advanced QI methods, such as tracking audit filters, complications, and statistical analyses, require more sophisticated medical record systems, often in the form of trauma registries. A trauma registry is a disease-specific database that captures uniform data elements, including injury events, demographics, prehospital information, diagnoses, care, outcomes, and treatment costs. These registries, typically computerized, facilitate data analysis and tracking of QI metrics. They are distinct from general medical records due to their ability to adjust for injury severity and focus on specific data elements. Trauma registries vary in inclusion criteria, data elements, and software used. For example, some registries include patients admitted for more than 24 hours, while others include all trauma deaths. Data collected may include injury severity scores, procedures performed, outcomes, complications, and resource utilization. Successful registries have been established in lowand middle-income countries using cost-effective or free software, such as Epi-Info. Examples include Uganda’s Kampala Trauma Score-based registry and Pakistan’s TRISS-adjusted registry. These efforts demonstrate the importance of improving data collection and use in QI activities. The appropriateness of QI techniques depends on the healthcare system level, trauma volume, and existing QI activities. For tertiary care centers with high trauma volumes, all QI techniques discussed in this text may be relevant. For smaller hospitals or networks of clinics, addressing trauma QI may still be important, especially for facilities along major roads. However, a dedicated trauma QI program may not always be warranted. Instead, broader management information systems addressing efficiency and quality improvement across various issues may be more suitable. Region-wide trauma QI efforts should consider the role of smaller facilities and their interaction with prehospital care. Preventable death panel reviews, including care providers from these facilities, can help identify problems and foster political will for corrective actions. The specifics of QI techniques will vary based on local considerations, but there is almost always a role for better monitoring of trauma care processes through QI activities. When initiating or expanding QI activities, two principles apply: building up slowly and sustainably, and engaging a range of stakeholders, including hospital administration, clinicians, prehospital providers, and governmental authorities. Adequate mandates and political support are essential for gathering necessary information and implementing corrective action plans. Finally, QI efforts for trauma care align with broader initiatives to strengthen healthcare management and patient safety. For example, WHO’s Patient Safety Programme and its “Safe Surgery Saves Lives” initiative promote standardized surgical safety checklists to reduce errors and improve communication. These efforts complement trauma QI goals, emphasizing the importance of safe operations as a key component of trauma care. Collaboration between patient safety and trauma QI advocates can drive organizational culture changes and political commitment to improve care quality and safety.
